newsitem.title: INDIA: India's "good neighbour" policy safe with Gujral.
newsitem.headline: India's "good neighbour" policy safe with Gujral.

text.p: The choice of Inder Kumar Gujral as India's next prime minister keeps peace talks with Pakistan on track, but question marks surround his economic policy and the life span of his disparate coalition.

Analysts said on Sunday the selection of the two-time external affairs minister as the successor to caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda virtually ensured the continuity of his foreign policy, dubbed the "Gujral Doctrine".
"As foreign minister, I have built some sort of a doctrine regarding neighbourly relations," Gujral told Reuters Television on Sunday. "That will continue to be my priority area."

The hallmarks of his policy, sketched out during the 10-month reign of Deve Gowda's government, were landmark water treaties with Bangladesh and Nepal, and the resumption of peace talks with Pakistan after a three-year period of acrimony.

The political crisis that erupted on March 30 when the Congress party revoked its make-or-break support for Deve Gowda's United Front coalition cast a shadow over high-level talks with Pakistan that were under way in New Delhi.

Now, talks between the prime ministers of India and Pakistan set to take place during a regional summit next month assume added importance as Gujral, who has spearheaded the drive to ease tensions with Islamabad, will represent Delhi.

In Islamabad, Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's press adviser Mushahid Hussain said Pakistan would welcome Gujral as prime minister, recalling a "cordial and pleasant" meeting between Gujral and Sharif, then in opposition, in 1995.

Hussain said Gujral "comes across as a person with a positive perspective on relations with Pakistan and we only hope that in his new position he will be able to translate that perspective into a practical policy".

"Gujral's Rise to Give Fillip to Indo-Pak Talks," said a headline in India's Pioneer newspaper, which called the prime minister-in-waiting "a politician, a statesman and a gentleman" with a healing touch.
The choice of Gujral brought a welcome end to India's three-week political crisis, but left many questions unanswered.

"Behind that collective sigh of relief lie vital and uneasy questions," wrote Indian Express editor Shekhar Gupta, noting the stormy departure of Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's regional Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) from the government.
The TMC backed out after left-wing parties in the United Front blocked its candidate for prime minister, G.K. Moopanar.

"Chidambaram's departure will send the wrong kind of signal to the rest of the world," Gautam Adhikari, former editor of the Times of India, told Reuters. "He had presented a face of India which is modern, progressive and open."

Chidambaram's investor-friendly budget, held hostage to the political turmoil, was to be taken up by parliament on Monday. While few doubted its ultimate passage, there were questions about Gujral's commitment to free-market economics.

"The antecedents are not very promising," said independent political analyst Rasheed Talib. "Will he be obliged to the left-wing parties which allowed him to win out against Moopanar? Is he willing to kick the ladder which he climbed to reach office?"
Adhikari said: "We don't know what his views are. I hope he will be strong enough to resist the influence of those who want to take the economy back to the pre-1991 days of big spending."

Gujral, 77, formed his world views during the Cold War, when he once served as ambassador in Moscow. "His old world values are positive in many ways, but I don't know if he has changed sufficiently to look at the world differently," Adhikari said.
Said a Western diplomat: "He hasn't exactly been a friend of the United States."

The United Front's competing ideologies and personalities which reared their heads during the three-week crisis, and the alliance's uneasy relations with Congress spell trouble for Gujral in the months ahead, the analysts agreed.
"I would expect a general election between October and December," Talib said. "I wouldn't give him a year."
